messages.content: Has anyone here build an analog-computer? Especially something like a Lorentz-Attractor? And if so, how did you build the sampling? Die-to-Die Bonding to a digital circuit or evaluation by oscilloscope?
there were like 3-ish hours of pause time in the middle as I was on a VC and it was lagging a bit too much.
Yeah, I'm working on an audio FPAA. 😎 We _could_ put converters on board, but right now ADCs/DACs are assumed external for ease/cost/fidelity. I/O is bidirectional analog pins.

Okay, so when you say audio, you are typically speaking less than 88kHz f_go, correct?
Do you have any idea on where I can find good data about die-to-die bonding of higher frequencies?

What is `f_go` in this context? The pole frequency caused by finite output conductance and the capacitance at that output? 

No idea. Die-to-die is planned, but no custom bonds, only the mini carrier boards with the default Wafer Space bonding option.
I'm guessing `f_g0` ?  Cross over frequency ?
I have DAC IP on my run 2 chips that I’ll get to test soon, I hope
May I ask what you're using for programmability? I happen to have a lot of experience in this specifically

it separates musician controls from correctness:
- routing: volatile config bits
- configuration: static bits
- calibration: DAC trimmers
- musical performance: continuous analog CV (lin/exp)
ahh okay it's digital controls
mostly
the lab I was doing research in was using analog floating gates for programmability
yeah, i was looking into FG, but decided against it for v1. mostly due to the programming speed
Let me DM you
Georgia tech ICE lab ?
Any chance you guys are planning on contributing back the numbers you guys will be collecting into the spice models @brookieoz ? 👀
I don't think anyone actually knows what the expected behavior of floating gates is apart from you guys.
Ah, I graduated in 2023. I haven't touched that stuff for years
Oh, that?
Fun, sorry, I just assumed you where part of the team that took part in run2.
When I was a student I was using FPAAs that were.... I think made in 2014?
If you wanted to model analog floating gates you basically use a gigantic resistor to set the DC point and tell SPICE to set that as your initial condition during a transient sim / etc
it is a bit risky though, sometimes you get hit with weird simulator errors because it doesn't solve correctly

@Tholin btw, I know you were having sim issue with diodes. I also ran into issues today but looks like there was some diode model rework in latest ngspice `main` branch and updating to that solved my convergence issues.
I’ve already fixed the problem on my end by eliminating diodes from my schematics
I know, it was just "for future reference" 😅
who sent the NS SAR and the DSM?

Wait a second, my battery charge controller chip is essentially just a linear voltage regulator with a current limiter and control state machine. If you ripped out just the linear regulator part of that, couldn’t you, say, generate a 3.3V core voltage on-die and have a single 5V power supply on a digital chip using my SCL?

I’d have to measure the dropout on the regulator to see what the true power supply range would be and maybe come up with a way of having a selectable 3.3V/5V IO voltage (though the former would be relatively weak coming from the internal regulator).

The power transistors for this would actually be quite small since the current consumption of standard cell logic, even for a dense 1x1 chip, should be pretty low. I think the full regulator could fit in a corner of the core area without taking up too much space. I’d have to use my run 2 chips to collect more data on my SCL.
If the 3.3V is also to supply the IO, it can be beefed up to 1A relatively easily while still not taking up too much space. For reference: my charge controller has a third of a 1x0p5 core area filled with just PFETs and that can conduct 110A according to SPICE. So, yeah, don’t need much FET to get 1A.
@Tim 'mithro' Ansell Is this worth investigating?
If yes, I’ll throw together a 3.3V regulator layout and use some of the unused pads on the charge controller chip to try it.

I think this would be cool - it's a small step from here to a SoC that can run straight off USB (you'd just need a 48MHz clock from somewhere to do data).  If you're doing that this offer might be of interest: https://discord.com/channels/1361349522684510449/1361349523724570941/1550939705410064526
What's your voltage reference ?
Bandgap reference
I simulated it across all process corners and varying supply voltages and temperatures and the total error was... I think less than 5%?
I don’t quite remember, I didn’t write the results down.
My SCL is characterized between 3V and 3.6V, so I have +/-10% error target
There is also a on-die oscillator I am testing on the charge controller chip, over in an unused corner. I have it set to 7.5MHz, but it has no temperature compensation, so it’ll drift a lot.
How much idk, I’ll just have to test it

I’m not sure I can take advantage of that offer since I’ve already done the top-level layout designed around a 1x0p5 slot. I would have to start completely over with all the layouts except for the analog building blocks to adapt to a different slot size and I just do not have the time.
Did some testing. You can get 1A with an array of 45 PFETs each 75u wide.
Just quickly generating that in magic, that’s 78u by 144u of area. Could probably shrink that height down a lot.

I quickly put together a schematic for such a voltage regulator.
Typical corner 27C: 3.301V
ff corner -40C: 3.588V
ss corner 125C: 3.014V
Interestingly its perfectly within the +/-10% range
But these conditions are also quite extreme. Especially on the COB boards will die long before 125C and the thermal stresses of cooling to -40C are probably also not going to be kind to it.
At the typical corner on a warm european summer day (40C) it sits at 3.27V, which is definitely good enough
1.5mA quiescent under those conditions
I'm sweeping the temp of the vref alone here and I get from 805 mv to 520 mv across -40 to 120.
so like +14% to -25% (across a very wide temp range for sure).
Right, I specified a much smaller temperature range when I tested it
I think only 0C to 70C
But in the results above you say -40 to 125, so I'm wondering how the output is more stable than the reference it uses.
Oh
No idea
Oh that’s... not right
Okay, maybe simulating a load and decoupling capacitor outside the chip is a good idea
That fixes things right up
And all is as it should be
Yes, internal regulators / supplies are still very much needed. Would be even better if they had a on/off switch.
I would like to see an internal 48MHz oscillator that feeds a PLL which uses the internal oscillator as the reference and trims using the USB data signal.

Uhhhhhhhh
Is that at weak hot corner?
with anything that's passing a decent amount of current you're gonna have to worry about metallization resistance and electromigration

I'm very unclear what type of timeline things like electromigration happen and if it matters for people who are only doing thousands of units with limited expected lifetime rather than hundreds of millions that need to have work for 30+ years.

Well, I agree that it's of less risk mostly because the stakes are a lot lower, but if you're not careful it can still bite you as EM is accelerated exponentially with increasing temperature, and poor power FET layout can encourage hotspots that make this failure more likely to happen
